assessment.nobel_worthiness: Built a systematic, formal and empirically testable framework for how constitutions, electoral rules and state capacity shape fiscal policy, public goods and growth. It opened a whole field and influenced work on institutions and development across many areas.
assessment.attribution: Persson and Tabellini are the clearest pair, with Besley closely tied through state capacity and political agency. Credit is concentrated and the three-person split is coherent. Acemoglu and Robinson, the nearest neighbours, are already recognised.
assessment.maturity: Decades of cumulative work, extensive replication and extension, and a settled place in textbooks and policy analysis. Timing is not a concern.
uncertainties: Some of the empirical constitutional-effects findings rest on observational variation and are contested.
Overlap with the 2024 institutions prize may lead some members to see the topic as already honoured.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The task-based view of technology and the trade-shock literature changed how economists understand labour demand, wage polarization and local labour-market adjustment to import competition. It combines credible quasi-experimental design with large social and policy impact, and it uses common-criteria evidence of the kind I find persuasive: new data plus an explanatory framework.
assessment.attribution: The China-shock evidence is most directly Autor, Dorn and Hanson. The task framework and technology-inequality work draw on Katz, Acemoglu (already a laureate) and Autor. Katz's inclusion would be reasonable, and my choice of three omits him.
assessment.maturity: About a decade and a half of replication, extensions and debate. The core findings have held up with refinements, and the long-run effects are now documented.
uncertainties: Debate continues about the magnitude and persistence of the China-shock effects.
Assigning credit for the task framework across Autor, Katz and Acemoglu is not clean.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Nominal rigidities, Calvo pricing, the Taylor rule and the Woodford-style microfounded framework form the backbone of modern monetary policy analysis and central-bank practice. The impact on policy is very large and sustained.
assessment.attribution: The list is crowded (Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Smets and others). Calvo (pricing), Taylor (rules and staggered contracts) and Woodford (synthesis and normative analysis) are the most separable, but the selection is contestable and could be seen as arbitrary.
assessment.maturity: Foundational contributions date back decades and have been extensively validated and used in practice. Timing is mature.
uncertainties: Difficult to limit credit to three people without excluding Gertler, Gali, Christiano and Eichenbaum.
Mixed empirical performance of the framework after the 2008 crisis and the post-2020 inflation.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Showed how collateral constraints turn small shocks into persistent, amplified fluctuations. This mechanism underlies much modern macro-finance and analysis of financial crises, and it is a clean, original theoretical insight with wide influence.
assessment.attribution: The 1997 paper is a clear two-author contribution. Gertler and Gilchrist are linked to the financial accelerator, and Bernanke, already a laureate, is a close neighbour. Two laureates give a tidy attribution.
assessment.maturity: Close to three decades of influence, reinforced by the 2008 crisis and quantitative extensions.
uncertainties: The framework is largely theoretical, and direct empirical confirmation is less clean.
Relationship to the 2022 banking and financial-crisis prize could weaken the case at the margin.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Population-scale administrative data transformed measurement of intergenerational mobility, neighbourhood effects and the design of opportunity policy. It is closely tied to my own field of administrative-data labour and crime research, so I weigh it cautiously to avoid favouring my own area. The data discovery combined with a conceptual framework meets the standards I value.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is central, with Hendren and Friedman as key collaborators on mobility and neighbourhood effects. Katz is credited for the Moving to Opportunity work. Attribution across a large team is a real concern, with Chetty overlapping the taxation candidate.
assessment.maturity: The core work is roughly 10 to 12 years old. Long-run validation of neighbourhood effects is still unfolding, and the field is young relative to typical Nobel timing.
uncertainties: Possibly too early for a decisive verdict on neighbourhood-effect findings.
Team-based credit and overlap with other candidates (B014).
Replication and causal interpretation of place-based estimates remain debated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Established that reciprocity and fairness concerns are systematic and formalised them in the Fehr-Schmidt inequity-aversion model. Evidence from experiments transformed work on contracts, public goods and cooperation, and has had a lasting effect on labour and organisational economics.
assessment.attribution: Fehr is the leading figure and Schmidt is the co-author of the key model. Falk is also central to the evidence base. A two-person award is plausible, while leaving Falk out is a judgement call.
assessment.maturity: Foundational work dates from the late 1990s, with a long record of replication and application. Timing is mature.
uncertainties: External validity of lab-based social-preference evidence is debated.
Behavioural economics has already been recognised (Kahneman, Thaler), so some members may see less room for another award.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Firm heterogeneity and selection reshaped trade theory and empirics by explaining who exports and how gains from trade arise within industries. It has a major impact on measurement and policy analysis.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the central contribution, and Helpman is linked to the broader heterogeneous-firm and new trade theory programme. Redding is more recent and quantitative. Krugman, who has already been recognised, and Grossman are also relevant.
assessment.maturity: More than two decades of consistent use, with strong empirical and quantitative extensions.
uncertainties: Overlap with Krugman's 2008 prize and with the Helpman-Grossman candidate (B044).
Credit relative to Bernard, Eaton, Kortum and others working on firms and trade.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Assembled long-run historical series on top incomes and wealth, which changed the way economists and policymakers see inequality. This is the kind of data-building plus explanatory-framework contribution I find compelling, though the theoretical framework is more contested than the data.
assessment.attribution: Piketty and Saez are the main authors of the top-income series, and Zucman extended the work to wealth and offshore holdings. Atkinson's earlier work is a related precursor, and Saez also appears in B014, so credit is entangled.
assessment.maturity: More than two decades of data work with wide influence. The theoretical claims (such as r > g) are less settled.
uncertainties: Debate about measurement choices and the interpretation of wealth-concentration trends.
Political salience may complicate assessment, although the committee evaluates scientific contributions only.
Overlap with the optimal-taxation candidate through Saez.
